subject: Re: Performance SLO & Concurrency requirements — Acme follow-up
thread_text:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Jensen <alice.jensen@acme.com>
Cc: Connor Obrien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 1 Oct 2026 14:05:00 -0700
Subject: Performance SLO follow-up / concurrency details (Acme)

Thanks again for taking the time today — great discussion. Quick recap + action items from our side and a few clarifying Qs so we can size the right Dedicated/quota profile and propose an initial pricing SOW.

Recap
- Target p95 generation latency: 150ms (you mentioned 100–150ms goal)
- Expected sustained throughput: ~500 requests/sec for the core inference path (20% streaming requests today)
- Peak bursts: ~1.5–2x sustained for short windows (a few minutes)
- Per-user concurrency: up to 3 parallel requests on heavy users; overall concurrency estimate ~1200 concurrent inflight requests

Questions (to confirm)
1) Average tokens per request and tokens/sec for streaming responses?
2) Split between streaming vs non-streaming calls (you mentioned ~20% streaming; please confirm)
3) Do you require persistent connection pooling (keep-alive) across thousands of clients, or will traffic originate from a smaller set of backend services?
4) Any hard constraints on throttling behavior for 429s vs queuing/backpressure?

Next steps
- If you can share the metrics snapshot (QPS by minute, tokens/request distribution) we'll run a concurrency/kv-cache sizing pass and return a config: target concurrency quota, recommended connection pool size, suggested burst buffer.
- I'll loop in Monica (CS) to coordinate an eval on Dedicated capacity and Connor for pricing.

Attachments: please attach the call metrics export if possible (timestamped minute-level).

Thanks — talk soon.

—
Marissa Cole
Sr. Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.ai | (415) 555-0192

From: Alice Jensen <alice.jensen@acme.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Bob Li <bob.li@acme.com>
Date: Thu, 1 Oct 2026 16:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Performance SLO follow-up / concurrency details (Acme)

Hi Marissa — thanks for the recap. Attaching the minute-level metrics export (acme-metrics-snapshot.csv). Answers inline below.

Answers:
- Avg tokens per request: 120 tokens (generation output), input tokens ~40. Typical response sizes 80–200 tokens.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: ~20% streaming today for low-latency UI; we expect to increase to ~35% over next quarter.
- Sustained throughput: Our current steady-state is ~450–550 RPS; target for Q1 is to be able to handle 700 RPS sustained.
- Peak bursts: We see up to 1,800 RPS for 3–5 minute windows during campaigns.
- Concurrency: From app-side tests, heavy users open up to 3 parallel requests; overall peak concurrent inflight requests around 1,400.
- Connection pooling: Traffic originates from ~120 backend app servers that maintain keep-alive pools. We maintain ~150–200 persistent outbound connections to the inference tier during peaks.
- Throttling behavior: Preference is graceful queuing where possible; 429s are acceptable only for sustained overload — we'd like a burst buffer to avoid rejecting short spikes.

Let us know what you recommend and any constraints from Redwood's rate limits or per-tenant quotas.

Thanks,
Alice Jensen
Platform Eng, Acme Corp
alice.jensen@acme.com

[Attachment: acme-metrics-snapshot.csv]

From: Connor Obrien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Jensen <alice.jensen@acme.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 2 Oct 2026 09:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Performance SLO follow-up / concurrency details (Acme)

Thanks Alice — this is super helpful. A couple quick clarifications so we size correctly:

1) For streaming requests: when you say 20% (rising to 35%), is the tokens/sec rate per streaming request similar to non-streaming (i.e., same total tokens but streamed), or do streaming sessions tend to be lower/higher tokens/sec? This affects KV cache hit behavior and batching.
2) For the 1,400 peak concurrent inflight: is that measured as in-flight model token-generation calls (i.e., a single concurrent request persists across streaming lifetime), or is it TCP-level connections?
3) Do you have a breakdown of request sizes by percentile (p50/p90/p99 tokens) in the attached CSV? If not, a rough estimate will do.

On the Redwood side, we have two relevant knobs we typically propose:
- Concurrency quota: tenant-level concurrency cap for inflight generation requests (prevents overload of model workers).
- Burst buffer: short-term request surge allowance that can exceed sustained concurrency for N minutes before shedding.

If you can confirm the above, we'll run load sims and propose a recommended quota + burst buffer and a rate-card.

—
Connor Obrien
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
connor.obrien@redwood.ai

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Jensen <alice.jensen@acme.com>
Cc: Connor Obrien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Sat, 3 Oct 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Performance SLO follow-up / concurrency details (Acme)

Alice / Bob — thanks for the metrics and answers. Based on the numbers we ran a quick sizing pass and a proposal below to avoid 429s during your spikes while meeting the p95 latency target.

Redwood proposal (initial sizing)
- Recommended sustained quota: 700 RPS (covers Q1 target)
- Recommended concurrency quota (inflight request slots): 1,200 concurrent generation requests
- Burst buffer: additional 600 slots for short windows (up to 5 minutes) to handle ~1,800 RPS spikes with soft queuing before shedding to 429s
- Connection guidance: support for 200 persistent outbound connections per tenant (your reported 150–200 is within this) — we recommend keeping client-side pools to ~2–4 connections per backend to avoid overloading the proxy layer.
- Streaming: Redwood's runtime provides streaming with KV-cache hot-warm behavior; we recommend enabling prefix caching for repeated prompts to reduce per-token latency.

Rate limits / quota notes
- Host-level token throughput limits still apply; we'll map your quota to a combination of concurrency + per-minute token limits. We'll propose the exact token rate after reviewing tokens/sec distribution from the CSV.
- For dedicated deployments we can set tenant-level quotas and configure a burst buffer policy that prefers queuing for up to 5 minutes, then gradually shed to 429s to preserve SLOs.

Next steps
1) Connor / Monica to run a short load sim using the attached CSV distribution and return an updated SLO config and an expected cost delta (we'll include this in the Redwood ratecard PDF).
2) We'll produce a draft SOW with pricing and SLO language, and a proposed rollout plan (canary -> linear ramp -> full).
3) If acceptable, we can schedule a 60m technical runbook session (Monica + your infra) next week to validate keep-alive sizing and network egress.

Attachments: redwood-ratecard-v2.pdf (initial pricing + quota templates).

If you'd like tighter p95 (e.g., 100ms), we can propose a higher-priority lane (lower batch sizes, reserved GPU capacity) — Connor can detail the cost impact.

Best,
Marissa

—
Marissa Cole
Sr. Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.ai | (415) 555-0192

[Attachments: redwood-ratecard-v2.pdf]
